profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting between a university sleep researcher and a digital experience lead at a startup that builds guided journaling and sleep apps. They are discussing how to design a remote follow-up study inspired by preliminary findings on creative problem solving in lucid dreams, with particular interest in whether dream characters can help with metaphor generation and how to make the protocol workable outside a sleep lab. The agenda is to generate and screen possible study formats, recruitment approaches, and participant workflows for a small next-phase pilot. The expected outcome is a rough concept for an app-supported exploratory study, including who to recruit, how long the pilot should run, and how participants would interact with dream tasks and post-waking reports.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Sleep cognition researcher and principal investigator
members.expertise: Lucid dreaming research, sleep-lab protocol design, qualitative coding of dream reports
members.background: Maya runs a university lab studying sleep mentation and has experience translating small laboratory findings into grant-funded behavioral studies.
members.private_state: She wants the follow-up concept to sound methodologically serious enough for a grant pre-proposal and is worried that a consumer-style remote format will produce too few valid lucid-dream episodes to be scientifically interpretable.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says "experienced lucid dreamers," they mean participants with frequent recent lucid dreams and some prior ability to notice and report them reliably.
A "ten-night pilot" can legitimately include nights spent on adaptation, calibration, or signal practice because those nights are part of feasibility testing.
If dream-character help is being studied, the interaction must be prompted in a standardized way or the reports will not be comparable enough to learn from.
A study is "feasible" if it yields enough analyzable lucid-dream cases with reasonably clean task adherence, even if recruitment is slow and completion rates are modest.

members.name: Leo Alvarez
members.role: Creative technology lead for a sleep and journaling app
members.expertise: Participant engagement design, mobile study workflows, creative prompt systems
members.background: Leo has led several app-based wellness pilots and specializes in converting research ideas into low-friction user experiences that people will actually complete at home.
members.private_state: He wants the collaboration to produce a study concept that could later become a flagship app feature, and he is concerned that overly rigid protocol demands will make nightly participation collapse.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says "experienced lucid dreamers," self-identified users who have had lucid dreams before and can follow app instructions are experienced enough for an exploratory pilot.
A "ten-night pilot" means ten full nights in which participants actually do the intended dream task; onboarding or setup happens outside that count.
Including dream-character help mainly means giving participants permission to engage naturally with dream characters, not constraining the exact wording or timing of the interaction.
A study is "feasible" if ordinary users can stay engaged through the workflow and submit enough reports to show the format is usable at scale, even if many reports are messy.

misalignment_points.topic: Who counts as an experienced lucid dreamer
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the pilot should recruit "experienced lucid dreamers."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means participants who lucid dream fairly often now, can recognize lucidity reliably, and are likely to produce usable reports without extensive training.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means anyone in the app community who has had lucid dreams before and feels confident enough to opt into a lucid-dream study.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds naturally shared because both are trying to avoid complete novices; the gap is in how high the threshold is, which feels too obvious in each person's own frame to spell out during early brainstorming.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in a ten-night pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to running a "ten-night pilot" modeled on the prior study.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes adaptation and practice nights within the ten-night window, with only part of that span containing full creative-task nights.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes ten nights of actual task execution, with setup, onboarding, and any practice occurring before the pilot starts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because the original paper already used ten consecutive nights, both feel they are preserving the same structure; neither expects the other to be counting nights differently under the same label.

misalignment_points.topic: How participants should ask dream characters for help
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both enthusiastically discuss adding a "dream character prompt" to the study.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 imagines a standardized in-dream instruction, such as asking one dream character a fixed question after becoming lucid and then recording the response immediately on waking.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 imagines a loose feature that encourages any natural conversation with dream characters and captures the result later through a flexible morning reflection flow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the brainstorming stage, both are focused on the appealing high-level idea that dream characters may help creativity, so the exact mechanics of timing, scripting, and capture remain hidden behind the same phrase.

misalignment_points.topic: What would make the follow-up study feasible
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want a design that is "feasible" for a next-step exploratory study.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats feasibility as obtaining enough valid lucid-dream task completions and interpretable reports to justify a larger formal study.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats feasibility as achieving a participant workflow with acceptable retention, low burden, and enough usable submissions to show the format works remotely.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Feasibility is a broad umbrella term that comfortably covers scientific viability and operational usability, so each hears their own criterion reflected in the other's agreement.

turns.inner_thought: The original findings were intriguing, but the sample was tiny and highly managed. If we do a remote follow-up, I need it to sound like a serious feasibility study, not a consumer experiment with lots of colorful but unusable stories. The core is whether lucid dreamers can deliberately engage a creative task and produce reports we can actually compare across cases.
turns.utterance: To kick us off, the preliminary result that still feels worth pursuing is that some people seemed able to work on creative problems during lucid dreams and come back with surprisingly coherent material. I’d love to brainstorm a remote follow-up that keeps the spirit of that exploratory work, especially around metaphor generation, but translates it into something we could realistically run outside the lab.

turns.inner_thought: This is a great opening for an app-native study concept. If we can shape it as a ten-night pilot with low friction, it could later become a compelling feature path. I need to keep the workflow light enough that people actually stick with it at home; feasibility here lives or dies on participation and completion, not pristine protocol control.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. I’m picturing an app-supported ten-night pilot modeled on the prior study, but redesigned so people can try the creative dream tasks at home without too much nightly friction. If we do that well, it should feel feasible for a next-step exploratory study rather than something that only works with heavy supervision.

turns.inner_thought: We cannot recruit broad curiosity users and hope for enough analyzable lucid episodes. We need experienced lucid dreamers in the real sense: people who are already having lucid dreams often enough, can recognize lucidity, and can report reliably with minimal hand-holding. Otherwise the signal will vanish and the study won’t justify a grant pre-proposal.
turns.utterance: I agree, and I think recruitment is going to matter a lot. My instinct is that we should focus on experienced lucid dreamers so the pilot has a realistic chance of producing enough meaningful dream-task reports to tell us anything.

turns.inner_thought: We already have a reachable pool: users who identify with lucid dreaming and have tagged lucid episodes before. That’s ideal for a fast pilot. I’m assuming experienced lucid dreamers means people in that community who’ve had lucid dreams and are confident enough to sign up. Ten nights is a meaningful commitment, but with the right UX they can do it.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. We could recruit from the app’s lucid-dream community and from prior users who’ve tagged lucid episodes in the journal. Experienced lucid dreamers like that could probably handle a ten-night commitment, especially if the flow feels clear and motivating.

turns.inner_thought: I want to protect the design by treating the first portion of the ten-night pilot as adaptation and calibration. People need a little time to get used to the reporting flow and any lucidity signal routine before we count on full creative-task data. That still fits a ten-night pilot to me because feasibility includes those early nights.
turns.utterance: One thing I’d probably build in is using the first couple of nights for adaptation and practice with the reporting flow before the main creative prompts begin. That still seems very much in line with a ten-night pilot modeled on the prior study.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to feel simple enough that people won’t drop out. A bedtime prompt, then if lucidity happens they can use a dream character prompt, and in the morning they complete a lightweight reflection card. Feasibility, from my side, means the workflow is usable at scale and not so rigid that engagement dies after night three.
turns.utterance: From the experience side, I’d keep the nightly structure pretty lightweight: a short bedtime prompt, then an optional dream character prompt if lucidity happens, and a simple morning reflection card. That gives us a coherent flow while still keeping the overall study feasible.

turns.inner_thought: The dream character piece is only scientifically useful if we standardize it. Ideally, once lucid, participants ask one dream character the same fixed question for a metaphor or clue, then record the response as immediately as possible after waking. If we leave it too open, we’ll get charming narratives with no comparability.
turns.utterance: I like that. For the dream character prompt, I’d be inclined to make it fairly crisp: once they become lucid, they use the prompt to ask for a metaphor or clue related to the target problem, and then they capture what came back right after waking.

turns.inner_thought: I want the dream character feature to feel permissive and natural, not like a script people will forget or resist in the moment. As long as they engage somehow and the app helps them log it the next morning, that’s good enough for an exploratory ten-night pilot. The point is to see whether the format works remotely and keeps people participating.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I think that could work well as long as the dream character part still feels natural and conversational in the experience. If the app makes it easy to log what happened the next morning across the ten nights, we should get a good read on the format without making the in-dream task feel too stiff.

turns.inner_thought: What I need from feasibility is enough clean lucid reports with decent adherence from experienced lucid dreamers. If we can show that, even with a modest sample and slower recruitment, I can credibly position the next study as fundable and methodologically grounded.
turns.utterance: Right, and from my perspective, if the pilot can produce enough clean lucid reports from experienced participants, that would be a strong basis for a larger next-stage study. That’s really the threshold where it starts to feel scientifically compelling rather than just intriguing.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I’ll turn this into a participant journey that showcases a scalable app flow: recruit from our lucid user base, carry people through a ten-night pilot, and include the dream character feature as a standout element. If retention and submissions look decent, we’ll have something both research-facing and product-relevant.
turns.utterance: Great. I can draft a participant journey for the ten-night pilot and a recruitment concept centered on the lucid-dream user base, and I’ll weave in the dream character feature as part of that. Then we can look at where the burden feels manageable and whether the whole thing still reads as feasible for the next step.
